title: Raj Kapoor
wiki_lead:
Ranbir Raj Kapoor (pronounced [raːdʒ kəˈpuːɾ]; born Shrishti Nath Kapoor; 14 December 1924 – 2 June 1988), popularly known as Raj Kapoor was an Indian actor and filmmaker who worked in Hindi cinema. He is considered to be one of the greatest and most influential actors and filmmakers in the history of Indian cinema. He has been referred to as The Greatest Showman of Indian Cinema as well as The Charlie Chaplin of Indian Cinema.
Born in Peshawar as the eldest son of Prithviraj Kapoor of the Kapoor family, Raj Kapoor starred in and produced many films for which he received multiple accolades, including three National Film Awards and 11 Filmfare Awards in India. He was inspired by Charlie Chaplin and played characters based on The Tramp in films, such as Awāra (1951), Shree 420 (1955) and Mera Naam Joker (1970). His performance in Awāra was ranked as one of the "Top-Ten Greatest Performances of All Time in World Cinema" by Time magazine in 2005. His films Awāra (1951) and Boot Polish (1954) competed for the Palme d'Or prize at the Cannes Film Festival in 1951 and 1955.
His films were global commercial successes in parts of Asia, the Middle East, the Caribbean, Africa, and the Soviet bloc. The Government of India honoured him with the Padma Bhushan in 1971 for his contributions to the arts. India's highest award in cinema, the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, was bestowed to him in 1988 by the Government of India.

Early life and background
Raj Kapoor was born as Shrishti Nath Kapoor on 14 December 1924 at Kapoor Haveli, a large house then owned by his grandfather in the Qissa Khwani Bazaar neighborhood of Peshawar, in the North-West Frontier Province of British India, into a Punjabi Hindu Khatri family. He had an Arya Samaji upbringing. His parents were Prithviraj Kapoor (3 November 1906 – 29 May 1972) and Ramsarni Devi Kapoor (née Mehra) (25 December 1908 – 14 June 1972). As per what Raj Kapoor's son Rishi Kapoor stated in his autobiography Khullam Khulla: Rishi Kapoor Uncensored, "It was he (Prithviraj Kapoor) who changed the family name from Nath to Raj, so that Prithvi Nath Kapoor became Prithviraj Kapoor. My father was named Shrishti Nath Kapoor at birth, but this was changed to Ranbir Raj Kapoor, which in turn became Raj Kapoor." Based on his father's name, Rishi Kapoor's son was named Ranbir Kapoor. The Kapoor family hailed originally from Samundri, a town in the Lyallpur District of the Punjab Province of British India (now in the Faisalabad District of Punjab, Pakistan).
Raj Kapoor was the eldest of six children in the family. He was the grandson of Dewan Basheshwarnath Kapoor, great-grandson of Dewan Keshavmal Kapoor, and great-great-grandson of Dewan Murli Mal Kapoor, and was part of the Kapoor family. His brothers were the late actors Shammi Kapoor (21 October 1931 – 14 August 2011) and Shashi Kapoor (18 March 1938 – 4 December 2017). He also had a sister named Urmila Sial (30 December 1933 – 25 July 2001). Two other siblings between Raj and Shammi, namely Devinder (Devi) and Ravinder (Nandi) died in infancy, within a gap of two weeks, both in the year 1931. Devi died of double pneumonia while Nandi died after accidentally swallowing rat poison while playing in the garden. Kapoor's family later on moved from Peshawar to Bombay for residence and for education.
As Prithviraj moved from city to city early in his career during the 1930s, the family had to move too. Raj Kapoor attended several different schools like Colonel Brown Cambridge School in Dera Doon, St Xavier's Collegiate School in Calcutta and Campion School in Bombay.


Extended family
He is the nephew of actor Trilok Kapoor, who is the younger brother of his father. His first cousin was director Vijay Kapoor who was the son of Trilok Kapoor and actor Subbiraj who was his father's sister's son. grok_lead: Raj Kapoor (14 December 1924 â 2 June 1988) was an Indian actor, filmmaker, and producer widely regarded as the "greatest showman of Indian cinema" for his innovative blend of social commentary, romance, music, and visual storytelling that shaped Bollywood's golden era. Born Ranbir Raj Kapoor in Peshawar, British India (now Pakistan), to renowned actor Prithviraj Kapoor and homemaker Ramsarni Devi, he grew up in a Punjabi Hindu family immersed in the performing arts, with his father founding the Prithvi Theatre troupe. After the Partition of India in 1947, the family relocated to Mumbai, where Kapoor began his career as a child actor and clapper boy before transitioning to leading roles in films like Neel Kamal (1947). In 1948, at age 24, he established R.K. Films and made his directorial debut with Aag, marking the start of his prolific output as a triple-threat talent who often starred in his own productions. Kapoor's signature style drew inspiration from Charlie Chaplin's tramp persona, portraying underprivileged everymen grappling with societal issues in iconic films such as Awara (1951), which explored class divides and became a global hit, and Shree 420 (1955), a satire on corruption that won a National Film Award for Second Best Feature Film. His works frequently incorporated lavish song-and-dance sequences and progressive themes, including interfaith romance in Bobby (1973)âa major directorial success without himself in the leadâand widow remarriage in Prem Rog (1982). Other landmarks include Barsaat (1949), his first major commercial success; Sangam (1964), a pioneering color love triangle; the semi-autobiographical Mera Naam Joker (1970); and Ram Teri Ganga Maili (1985), which earned him a Filmfare Award for Best Director. Over his 40-year career, Kapoor helmed around 20 films, many achieving international recognitionâ Awara and Boot Polish (1954) were nominated at the Cannes Film Festival, while Jagte Raho (1956) secured the Crystal Globe at Karlovy Vary. He amassed three National Film Awards, 11 Filmfare Awards (including lifetime achievement posthumously), the Padma Bhushan in 1971, and the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 1987, India's highest cinematic honor, which he received amid health struggles from chronic asthma. Married to Krishna Malhotra since 1946, with whom he had five children including actors Randhir and Rishi Kapoor, he built a cinematic dynasty that endures today, including the 2025 relaunch of R.K. Studios by his grandson Ranbir Kapoor. Kapoor's death from asthma-related complications at age 63 left an indelible mark, with his films continuing to symbolize Bollywood's humanistic ethos and inspire filmmakers worldwide.
